items.question: How do you see compute constraints shaping the benefits of automating AI research and development?
items.object: Compute scaling and the automation of AI research and development
items.answer: If I take this compute scaling view seriously, maybe each order of magnitude of effective compute scaleup gets you some additional percentage of tasks that are automated in the economy until you've automated everything. Even if you do automate R&D, it's not clear how much that gets you. If you think the scaling of compute has been the key driver of the rapid software progress over the past 10 to 15 years, then you wouldn't necessarily be resolving that bottleneck by just scaling the researcher population much faster.

items.question: How do you think about forecasting the trajectory of AI development?
items.object: Forecasting AI development and economic feedback loops
items.answer: I don't think extrapolation works very well. In 2015, 2016, self-driving cars were maybe the most exciting application. Well, 10 years later, the story is the LMs and reasoning models, and OpenAI forecasts a hundred billion dollars per year of revenue by 2029. But that's not anywhere near enough for the economic feedback loops to become intense enough. If you want this sort of feedback loop that goes from increased economic output to more AI developments, more scaling, then you need the economic output to actually be scaling quite rapidly. What matters is what are the broader incentives and forces? What are those forces pushing AI to be like?

items.question: Why did you develop GATE to model economic decisions about AI automation differently from Tom Davidson’s earlier model?
items.object: GATE’s approach to modeling economic decisions about AI automation
items.answer:
So there was this previous line of work done by Tom Davidson at Open Phil, where he basically translated the idea of compute scaling into a setting of an economic model. He says, okay, there's some spectrum of tasks in the economy. If he takes this compute scaling view seriously, maybe each order of magnitude of effective compute scaleup, allowing for software progress as well as just physical compute scaling, gets you some additional percentage of tasks that are automated in the economy until you've automated everything. There's a certain slope for when you start automating tasks. Each order of magnitude, you automate maybe 10%, maybe 20% of the tasks in the economy, and then you can plug that assumption into a relatively standard economic model, which turns into a nonstandard model because most of these models don't have AI in them. But the rest of the model can be fairly standard, like the production function and how you assume that investments and consumption and whatever decisions in the economy are made. Tom Davidson's original model was also developed with Epoch assistance, especially on the software side, and then we decided to develop GATE because that model had some shortcomings that we wanted to address.

Maybe the biggest one was that in that model, economic decisions were hardcoded. They were not made in the standard way that this would typically be done in the economics literature, which would be that you would have some kind of utility or value function, and then you would be optimizing that to get the best outcome, maybe under certain constraints. Instead of doing that, it was just a bunch of hardcoded rules, little parameters that I think the Open Phil folks just thought made sense. But that meant if you used relatively extreme parameter values or something, the decisions would look very unreasonable. So that was the main motivation to turn it into a standard economic model. This would also allow us to answer questions that the original model could not. You could say, okay, suppose that people assign such-and-such credence to AGI being capable of full automation, let's say 10%. They're not sure, maybe they're uncertain. Then what should they do? How much should they invest? There are these interesting possibilities where people might invest a bunch early if that helps them resolve the uncertainty. Maybe they observe the slope of the automation curve to see, okay, does this thing look like it's going to get full automation? Maybe it does, maybe it doesn't.

So they might update on that, and that might inform their investment decisions, which we can observe in GATE, which you couldn't observe in this older framework because all the decisions had been hardcoded. So that's the basic motivation.

items.question: How do you think GATE should be used to improve people’s thinking about AI?
items.object: GATE’s value as a tool for clarifying beliefs about AI
items.answer: It's important to not oversell the model in the sense that it's not really meant to be a predictive model. It's meant to be more like, as I think Tom Davidson's original model was, not really meant to be predictive. In fact, a lot of economics models are not really meant to be predictive. They are more meant to show you what happens in this simulated world where certain mechanisms are built into the world and certain ones might be left out. But I think a lot of people's thinking about AI can be incoherent in the sense that they might believe things that are actually incompatible with each other, and this kind of model helps clarify that.

items.question: What do you see as the main value of using the GATE economic model to reason about AI automation timelines?
items.object: The GATE model's value for reasoning about AI automation timelines
items.answer:
One example would be that you might have certain beliefs about how fast software progresses, how much we're going to be able to scale up investments, or, for example, you might have beliefs about how fast we can double our stock of compute or our number of fabs or whatever without running into severe constraints, like serial time constraints or something. And you might not notice how aggressive the combination of those beliefs should actually make you about timelines. When you put all of that into a model, you might be surprised by how fast the automation actually happens. The main benefit of the model that I see is, instead of you having to reason about this in your head, where you think, okay, let me take this into account and this other thing and this other thing, and then let me just think about what would happen, you might have a bias in either direction when you're doing that.

When you have the model, it just clarifies your thinking, because either you have to disagree with the model's parameters, and then you can delve into that: okay, I disagree with this parameter value, so then what evidence do we have about that particular parameter value? For example, one parameter that's important in the model is: if we double our instantaneous research efforts, if you have twice the number of resources working on software R&D or hardware R&D, then how much faster would we be making progress, at least at that moment? That is not clear. It's not necessarily that if you double your researcher stock, you make twice as fast progress, because some things could just be difficult to parallelize. And then there's this penalty. There might also be another question about what if you spend twice as much instead of having literally twice as much resources, in which case you might also have to think about the price impact. Maybe as you try spending more, the supply is limited. So you're running up against the constraints on the supply of competent researchers, in which case you might even get less of an impact than you thought.

And then you might notice that these parameters actually look quite important, because if you could increase our spending by 10x and that got us 10x faster software progress, maybe we would be doing that. There's a separate effect about this fishing out: as you make progress in any domain of R&D, making further progress might become harder. So then you might ask, what is the size of that effect? There are lots of things like this that might become relevant when you have a model like this and you do a sensitivity analysis on the model, and you notice that some parameters are very important for explaining the model's predictions about timelines, but maybe other ones don't matter that much. Then you can focus on the ones that do matter.

items.question: Why do you think the degree of complementarity in the economy matters for AI timelines in Epoch’s GATE model?
items.object: Economic complementarity in Epoch’s GATE model
items.answer: I would say the degree of complementarity in the economy at large matters, because what this means is, suppose that AI automates 50% of tasks in the economy instead of 100%. How much of a boost to output does that give you? If it gives you a lot, then that actually speeds up the process because you have this expanded pool of output that you can reinvest into more chips and more R&D and stuff like that, and that gets the entire feedback loop to happen faster and it can end up shortening timelines.

items.question: How do you think the time required to build physical infrastructure could constrain the pace of AI scaling?
items.object: Adjustment costs and physical infrastructure timescales as constraints on AI scaling
items.answer: I would say what we would call adjustment costs or timescales, like the serial time constraints in building a new fab, or maybe also just for ordinary kinds of physical capital investments, like building power infrastructure and things like that. We don't know to what extent there are just serial time constraints in that process, so even if you try to do that much faster at our current level of technology or maybe slightly above it, we might not be able to do it that much faster. There's a question about the scaling curve. Imagine you spend twice as much to get something done faster, like get a power plant to be built faster. Well, maybe that doesn't actually get you to the finish line that much faster than you might expect. Maybe there are just some limits there. If there are limits, then those things can just become bottlenecks and sort of determine the overall pace at which you can continue scaling. It might become even more of an issue in the future, when we will actually need to scale other things. Right now I think we're only really having to construct data centers, and maybe we are having to worry about power. But in the future, especially if you want this sort of feedback loop that goes from increased economic output to more AI developments, more scaling, then you need the economic output to actually be scaling quite rapidly if you want that to be effective. That is just going to be bottlenecked by these things if you can't do them. So it's quite important that we scale those things reasonably fast.

items.question: How do you assess the amount of effective compute needed for full automation in Epoch’s GATE model?
items.object: The effective compute requirement for full automation in Epoch’s GATE model
items.answer:
An important parameter is how much effective compute is required to get to full automation. That's just always an important parameter, because that tells you how much distance there is that you have to cross. If that number is very high, then you might not see much economic impact from AI at all. But we have these arguments; there's a whole literature about trying to estimate this number that came out even before Tom Davidson's model. There's the Bio Anchors report from Ajeya Cotra, which tries to estimate this number in a bunch of different ways. I think it's not super plausible that this number is much larger than what we allow for in the model. I think maybe it's like 10 to the 40 FLOP or something, effective FLOP, but I don't think it's much larger than that, because that ends up being in tension with the evidence we have from, say, evolution.

Human brains are effectively AGI, you could say, and there was a certain amount of computation that went into producing the human brain as an artifact. Evolution is probably less efficient than the machine learning process that we're engaged in.

I mean, there are some ways evolution might have advantages because it has a lot of serial time, which we don't have. It has hundreds of millions of years, while we usually need to do things in a much more compressed time frame. It also has the ability to collect real-world data, which in a bunch of ways you might be bottlenecked by in the future. So I don't want to totally overstate the case, but I think something like this is probably true. For the model, I think in the main line we maybe assume 10 to the 36 FLOP is the default parameter setting in the model. If you work with that and make the full assumptions about everything else, maybe you get timelines of 10 or 15 years. Timelines to what? Timelines to full automation. And we get timelines to begin seeing quite a lot of economic impact even three or four years out.

items.question: What concerns do you have about how Epoch’s GATE model represents software R&D as progress toward AGI?
items.object: The GATE model’s treatment of software R&D as progress toward AGI
items.answer:
I think this is a tricky domain where we're using this abstraction of effective FLOP. Basically, we're assuming that software progress acts sort of like it cuts the compute cost of building the system that is capable of automation, or in fact building any system at any level of capability: you get this factor of cost saving. I think that's not necessarily a realistic model in a bunch of different ways. One of them is that software progress is not uniform across scales like that. Maybe it works more and maybe it's stronger for models trained on more compute compared to less compute, but we don't know that. There's no decisive evidence about that.

I would be more worried that our software R&D estimates are very much calibrated on domains like computer vision and language modeling at something like the current level of capabilities. Maybe that means we are making progress towards this more general level of capabilities as well, that you might call AGI, at the same rate. Maybe we were even going faster there, but maybe we're going slower.

For example, if you looked at chess engines in the 1990s, we were making some software progress. You wouldn't have said that that software progress was actually getting us closer to AGI in a meaningful way, because that task just seems too narrow and too limited for us to use that. Maybe that's the case with AGI even today. That would be, I think, the big argument, if true, because if you take away the software R&D channel, that costs you quite a lot of orders of magnitude of effective FLOP. It has the same effect as if you increase the training requirements for AGI, because you lose the support from software.

items.question: How do you assess whether the fast rate of software progress in language modeling reflects progress toward AGI?
items.object: Extrapolating language-model software progress to progress toward AGI
items.answer: Well, it's more plausible than it is for chess. I'm not sure if the rate of progress towards an AGI system is actually in line with the rates we estimate for language modeling, which are quite fast. Usually they're on the order of 3x per year or something like that. Is that right? I don't know. That rate couldn't have continued for a very long time, because if you extrapolate that backward, then you begin to reach these implausible conclusions. If you extrapolate that by 30 or 40 years backward, then you get the conclusion that back in 1980 or 1990 or whatever, we would have needed more compute to come up with the algorithm of the human brain than evolution used for all evolution, and that just doesn't seem plausible. So you can get around that by saying that we only have this fast rate of progress since 2012 or 2015 or something, basically only in the deep learning era, and that era is short enough that you don't have this implausible conclusion.

items.question: Why do you think limits to compute scaling could slow progress toward AGI?
items.object: Compute scaling as a potential bottleneck on software progress and AGI development
items.answer: If the rate of progress has only lasted for a short time, and the short time period coincides with the period in which we've been rapidly scaling compute, it suggests a different thing that might become the obstacle, which is that maybe software progress is bottlenecked on using compute for experimentation. That's why we're seeing this rapid progress in software just as we're scaling compute very aggressively, and why we didn't see this in other domains, or we didn't do the same thing, or we've just relied on Moore's law. Effectively, our budgets remained fairly fixed and then we relied on Moore's law. We should expect progress to stall because we can't keep scaling compute at the rate that we're currently scaling compute, unless AGI is fairly soon and then these other economic feedback loops kick in and allow us to continue it. But, assuming that doesn't happen, we're probably going to run out of runway to do that by 2030 at current rates. Then compute scaling will have to slow down, just because the spending on clusters and training runs will become so exorbitant that we will not be able to scale it any further with our current pool of resources and willingness to invest. So I think it is an important question in general, aside from anything to do with GATE: whether we reach this point before 2030 or not. items.question: Why do you doubt that automating AI research alone would be enough to sustain rapid AI progress through the end of the decade?
items.object: Automating AI research as a way to sustain rapid AI progress
items.answer:

Even if you do automate R&D, it's not clear how much that gets you if you can't automate the scaling of compute. If you think the scaling of compute has been the key driver of the rapid software progress over the past 10 to 15 years, then you wouldn't necessarily be resolving that bottleneck by just scaling the researcher population much faster. There's a question about to what extent research efforts from humans or possibly AIs, compute for useful experiments, and maybe to some extent real-world data, insofar as that matters, are complements. I would assume that these are complements, and if you just scale one of them by orders of magnitude while the other one remains flat, then you're just going to get bottlenecked and it's not going to have as big of an impact as you might have thought.

items.question: How do you understand Dario Amodei, Demis Hassabis, and Sam Altman’s views on how AI will create economic value?
items.object: AI company leaders’ views on AI’s economic value through research and development
items.answer:
I mean, they probably do put a lot of emphasis on that channel of AI automating its own R&D, but they also generally emphasize R&D, which is a different thing. They're saying that AI will mainly produce this value by automating the process of R&D in general, and then it's going to make a lot of scientific contributions. A paradigmatic example here might be AlphaFold, or things like AlphaProof or AlphaGeometry, which is not really doing science. They tend to be very optimistic. Definitely Dario is saying, “Oh, it's going to happen in two years,” and so I'm clearly saying something else. You might ask, so why is he so optimistic? Sam has sometimes expressed views that are more mixed. He has said, “Oh, we will have AGI and then it will not be that big of a deal; the world will sort of continue.” That's a very different view. Demis is much more excited about applications of AI for science, revealed in DeepMind's research priorities. AlphaFold was a DeepMind effort, AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry are DeepMind efforts, AlphaGo was a DeepMind effort.

I think AlphaGo is obviously not science, but you can see that it was informed by this view that we need to do this reinforcement learning thing, and we need AI that can do complex reasoning and solve complex problems, instead of the usual training pipeline that's common today. items.question: How do you understand the main mechanism behind the massive economic impact projected by the GATE model of AI development?
items.object: The mechanism behind GATE’s projected economic impact
items.answer:
GATE doesn't have what you would call an endogenous growth model in the general economy, which would mean that productivity in the general economy increases as a result of research effort or investment. That's just assumed to be either flat or maybe growing at some exogenous rate that's fairly slow. But GATE still produces massive economic impact. It's very simple. You have all these AI workers, and that effectively gives you this massive scaleup in your effective labor force by many orders of magnitude. Right now, if you look at the key bottlenecks in the world economy, the most important input is labor. Labor is paid something like 60 or 65% of all income as wages. If you look at gross domestic product or gross world product and how much goes to paying labor, it's like 65%. It's the dominant contribution. Of the remaining 30%, capital is something you can also scale: you can reinvest your output into producing more factories and more machine tools and whatever. That's also something you can scale. Right now we can't scale labor; we can't reinvest our output to produce more workers. We just have to rely on human population growth.

But if we were able to do this for AI workers, that would enable us to dramatically scale them in a way we can't do for humans. You would end up in a world where you have maybe a thousand AI workers for each human, let's say. It's very easy to see how that would produce a dramatic change in standards of living and productivity and everything. I think that's the key mechanism that's happening in GATE. In that respect, GATE is actually a conservative model because it's not modeling the fact that you would also get this general feedback loop from all this increased capacity and thinking ability back into productivity, which would also increase productivity a bunch. That effect is not smaller than the effect in GATE, but most of the effect is actually coming from the labor force, because economic output is much more elastic to labor force scaling than it is to R&D. That's the dominant thing. R&D matters for long-run growth: if you don't do any R&D, eventually you run into the limits of your current technology, or if you don't do any learning by doing or discoveries. If productivity remains flat, eventually you run into the limits of your technology. But most of the economic impact is not coming from the increase in productivity, in the sense of total factor productivity the way an economist would use the term. It's coming from this massive scaleup.

items.question: Why do you think people overestimate R&D’s contribution to long-run economic growth?
items.object: R&D’s contribution to long-run economic growth
items.answer:
For long-run economic growth, you need to be scaling all factors of production at once. Total factor productivity is just one factor of production in the way we think about it in growth economics. Labor and capital are also important factors of production. Labor is probably the most important, and then capital and total factor productivity. If you look at the actual returns that you get when you're scaling them, they seem to be about equally important or something. If you do growth accounting, what you find is that total factor productivity growth is only a fraction of long-run growth. The part of that driven by explicit R&D instead of things like learning by doing or economies of scale—you're just more efficient at producing things because you operate on a larger scale—or better management, better coordination, less misallocation of resources: all those things affect productivity. The part driven by explicit R&D is a fraction. Basically, the part of economic growth driven by R&D directly is a fraction of a fraction of all economic growth.

So it ends up being fairly small compared to what people think, which is that almost all of it is driven by R&D. That's not true. But I think people can misunderstand this claim and say, “Well, if you didn't have any R&D, we wouldn't have grown since the 1700s, and we wouldn't have our current level of wealth and prosperity.” That's true, but that just means R&D is essential for long-run growth. A lot of other things are also essential. Imagine that we had done R&D since 1700 but hadn't scaled our capital stock at all. We would again be very poor now.

It's possible that even though a job is very valuable, it's actually very expensive to do it, so you don't end up deploying the AI to do that. But if you assume that AI costs a certain amount and is capable of doing any job in the economy, then you would deploy it at the highest-compensated jobs. In fact, this bottleneck is likely to matter at least early on because we don't have that much compute worldwide. Even in these countries we don't have that much supply of compute to be able to do it freely. So you'd still be targeting the occupations that have the highest compensation because that would make economic sense from the point of view of the labs.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between R&D's social value and AI labs' incentives to automate it?

items.answer: I see a sense in which even the social value of R&D, which does exist and is essential for long-run growth, even if it's not literally the most important thing that drives it, is still a key bottleneck that we need to get past. Even that social value is mostly external, which means that if you're an AI lab, you don't get most of the value from doing the R&D. Software R&D is a bit different because you internalize the value at least to some extent. There are multiple competitors, so you don't totally internalize it, but to some extent. items.question: Why do you think saving and investing more is a good personal strategy for a gradual AI-driven economic transformation?

items.answer: From a personal perspective, I would just say that probably saving more and investing more is a good bet. If you already have a certain amount of income today, you can't really get that much more by having more. The scale of our economy and the level of our technology only allow us to produce goods of a certain variety, and there are a lot of goods or services that we can't offer. I think these are small things; there are probably a lot of other varieties of goods that are going to come up.

items.question: How do you understand the prospect of human wages falling below subsistence in an AI-driven economy?
items.object: Human wages falling below subsistence in an AI-driven economy
items.answer: Unemployment just means that you're looking for a job but don't like the offers on the market. That is probably what would happen, in the sense that people's wages would fall to the point where it is no longer worth it. Your wages could fall below subsistence, and then there's no point in working in that world. Either you have some wealth or you rely on various kinds of transfer programs, which would give you way more income than you would be able to get just by working. That's the kind of thing I would expect. Economically, it's a complex question. I think it's much easier to predict that eventually wages are going to fall below subsistence, at least for biological humans, than to predict when that will happen. As you scale up your capital and labor stock, you hit diminishing returns that lower the marginal value of those things, and wages are just the marginal product of labor. So you expect those to fall, but at the same time there's an opposing effect because you're going to be getting increased total factor productivity, and that could cancel the falling wages you would otherwise expect from the increase in labor, at least up to a certain point. It also depends on how fast the world economy grows, because the faster we grow, the faster we reach the bottlenecks. items.question: How do you think workers will fare as AI progresses toward full automation?

items.answer: So the point I was making is that extrapolation just doesn't work very well. In fact, it doesn't work well in a lot of other, very basic ways. items.question: How would you approach training a transformer to become more agentic or capable of long-term planning?

items.question: How do you understand Moravec's paradox in terms of how well optimized different human capabilities are?
items.object: Moravec's paradox and variation in human skill
items.answer:
Moravec's paradox is the observation that perception and sensorimotor skills are much more computationally expensive and difficult than skills that typically seem to us to be associative intelligence, like playing chess. It's a very old observation. The basic explanation Moravec himself gave for the paradox is that the capabilities that seem difficult to us are the capabilities that are new and not very well optimized in us. Humans were not selected for their ability to play chess, so we can have vast variations in the efficiency with which we play chess. If you look at the point at which AI systems or computers reached medium, amateur strength in chess, like 1200 or 1300 ELO, that was around when we were using a certain amount of compute. Then look at how many orders of magnitude of scaling we had to do until we reached the level of the world champion, around 2800 ELO. We had to do around five orders of magnitude of physical compute scaling and a bunch of software progress.

If I look at it naively, that says the human range in chess-playing ability is at least more than five orders of magnitude wide, from median to right tail, and then there's the left tail, which is maybe even worse, maybe some orders of magnitude worse. Imagine if you had six orders of magnitude of variation between people in how fast they could run. That would be very strange; it's not something you would expect. We say some people run faster than others.

items.question: Why do you see evolution's influence on the human brain as analogous to algorithm architecture search?
items.object: Evolution as algorithm architecture search for the human brain
items.answer:
The point is that if doing a task was very valuable in the evolutionary environment and has been valuable for a very long time, then there's been a lot of selection pressure applied. The way those capabilities are instantiated or implemented in the human brain—the algorithms used to do those things—are very sophisticated. You don't get a lot of trained parameters or whatever from evolution, because DNA doesn't contain that much information. DNA only contains enough information to code for an algorithm and high-level details. I wouldn't view evolution as analogous to a training run, with the results going into your brain, because there isn't that much information in the genome. But you can view it as analogous to algorithm architecture search.

The algorithms are very separate. The brain has different regions responsible for different things: the cerebellum has its own responsibilities, separate from the rest of the brain. It has specific areas devoted to visual processing, audio processing, general-purpose thinking in the prefrontal cortex, language understanding, and parsing. These are all very regional and probably done by different kinds of algorithms to some extent, because they're regional and the same areas are in everyone. It has to be coded in the genome somewhere that that's how it happens.

items.question: How do you explain the wide variation in human chess ability compared with sensorimotor skills?

Because it hasn't been optimized, there's a lot of room to improve the efficiency with which you make use of the brain's resources, its power usage and computational power, to get better performance on a task.

If you stack all those up, you end up with this five or six orders of magnitude difference in efficiency of people playing chess. items.question: How do you assess the potential for AI to automate management?
items.object: AI automation of management
items.answer:
People differ enormously in their ability to do management. A typical person put in charge of a company of any meaningful scale would probably be destructive. They would add negative value to the company, interfere with what it's doing in harmful ways, and mess things up. It's not very natural to expect that. Then you have this right tail of people who are extremely effective at doing it. If there's such vast variation, that's a generic reason to expect that there's at least a big component of the task that's easy for AIs. That doesn't mean the entire task is easy for AIs, because management does require long-context understanding and things like that, which I think load on human skills that are older. But you would try to get the AI to automate as much of your work as you can, especially the parts that rely on newer skills that you aren't actually that good at. That might improve the quality.

Even if AI were capable of substituting for human managers, I think we would probably stick with human managers for at least a while for social, political, and legal reasons. You want someone to be liable for decisions, and it's easier if it's a human compared to an AI, but also for social reasons.

items.question: Why do you consider a 75% score on FrontierMath, your advanced mathematics benchmark, an impressive but reasonable prospect for AI models?
items.object: The difficulty of FrontierMath and the prospect of AI models scoring 75% on it
items.answer:
FrontierMath is a benchmark that we created in collaboration with OpenAI. It consists of math problems at least an order of magnitude harder than previous math benchmarks, and maybe even more. The harder questions might be two orders harder in terms of how long it would take an expert human to solve them. They also require specialized domain knowledge for the harder questions. Maybe 25% of the benchmark could be done in 30 minutes by a person with a math competition background. The medium questions would likely take an hour or two, and the hardest questions would take even longer and require more background.

The current state-of-the-art score in our own evaluations is about 11%. OpenAI has its own internal evaluations where it reports much higher scores, but those are for models not released to the public: models like o3, which OpenAI said got 25%, or o3 mini high evaluated with much larger inference budgets and custom internal scaffolding that OpenAI doesn't expose to external users, with which they claim to get around 30%.

In our own evaluation, we evaluate models as they exist: subscribe to OpenAI, go to their API, pick o3 mini high, use our own custom prompting, and give the model access to tool use. Our way of giving it access to tool use is probably not as sophisticated or performant as OpenAI's. That's what FrontierMath is. I think 75% on that benchmark is quite an impressive score, but I don't think it's unreasonable. I think it's in line with what other people expect, because reasoning RL is such a new paradigm and it's nowhere near saturated. People are spending quite a bit less on it, maybe 10x or more less, than on pretraining. There's still a lot of room for them to scale it up.

items.question: Why do you think advertised context-window sizes fail to capture how well language models actually handle long texts?
items.object: Language models’ advertised context windows and long-context evaluations
items.answer: Currently the models' performance degrades quite a lot if you try to use them in any kind of longer context. It's not just about the context window limits you see, like, “We can only handle 200,000 tokens in one context.” That's fake. They can't handle 200,000 tokens without loss of performance. The benchmarks they have for testing long-context performance are very narrow. They're things like needle-in-a-haystack evaluations, where you just have to find some specific thing in a long passage of text. But what matters more is: if I give you a long document, how much do you hallucinate about it? How much do you understand if different parts of it are interacting with each other? If you talk with a language model over a long context—for example, have it write a story for you—you'll notice that even after you get past tens of thousands of tokens, low tens of thousands, its coherence and ability to understand what's going on, recall details, and make inferences based on what has been written in the past context starts getting worse. I don't know how this will be solved. Maybe it will be solved by fine-tuning on more long-context things.

items.question: Why do you see reliable long-context performance as an important bottleneck for economically valuable AI applications?
items.object: Reliable long-context performance as a bottleneck for economically valuable AI applications
items.answer: I'm not sure what the key thing is going to be, but it seems like a big issue because long context is required for unlocking a lot of economically valuable applications. Even 200,000 tokens is not that long. That's not enough to fit a good chunk of Harry Potter books; you can fit a single book into a context. That makes it much more annoying to use. If these models had tens of millions of tokens of context and could do that without noticeable loss in performance, and maybe without a steep increase in price, which is what you might get today because of the complexity of attention, I think that would be valuable and unlock a lot of other economically valuable applications. items.question: How do you think about using recent AI progress to predict when AI will fully automate remote work?

items.answer: So I think that a lot of people have this intuition that progress has been very fast. They look at the trend lines and just extrapolate; obviously, it's going to happen in, I don't know, 2027 or 2030 or whatever. They're just very bullish. And obviously, that's not a thing you can literally do. There isn't a trend you can literally extrapolate of “when do we get to full automation?” Because if you look at the fraction of the economy that is actually automated by AI, it's very small. items.question: How do you think someone outside an intellectual community can use the internet to find people worth learning from?

items.answer: I think the internet is a pretty useful thing in this respect. You don't need to necessarily talk to people, you can get a lot of benefit from reading. But you just need to identify, who are the people who seem constantly most interesting? And maybe you find one person. And then often that person will know some other people who are interesting. And then you can start tracing the social network. One example I can give, which I think is actually accurate, is maybe you know about Daniel Ellsberg. So you look for a podcast he appears on. You notice that he's appeared on 80,000 Hours podcast, which he has. And then you notice there are some other guests on the 80,000 Hours podcast. So maybe there's Bryan Caplan, who has also appeared on the podcast. And then maybe Robin Hanson has also appeared on the podcast. And then maybe there are some people those other people know. And then just tracing that kind of social network and figuring out who to listen to like that. And I think you're doing a very big service to making that possible. I think your selection is often very good.
